R² cases 0.488 vs Python 0.501; ESS_kish 65.5 vs 57.6/59.7. Done this way because no archived Python-engine run is reachable and C-1 removed the engine="python" path that could produce one; the substitute is better controlled, since an archive would also differ in data vintage, priors version and package version. One real behavioural difference found — see below
A-5 engine difference: prior-tail admissibility found, quantified, not a defect — NumPy’s Poisson raises ValueError('lam value too large') above λ ≈ 9.2e18 because it returns int64; R’s rpois() returns a double and handles it correctly (relative sd 2.9e-11 at λ = 1e21 against the expected 3.16e-11). So 13 of 500 prior draws (2.6%) run in R and are rejected by Python — the same 13 in both Python replicates despite a 100,000 seed offset, i.e. deterministic in the draw, not stochastic. All 13 carry an extreme zeta_2 (up to 1.4e15) and the shedding draw is what overflows. The R results for them are sane (no NAs, 0.5–6.4M cases against 2–3.8M for the best ordinary draws), they would carry 3.2% of posterior mass, and one ranks 9th best of 500 — so this reaches the posterior and is not dismissible as deep-tail noise. Tier C cannot see it at all, because it holds parameters fixed and varies only the seed; it surfaces only when draws sweep the prior. R is the correct arm here, so the practical effect is that the R engine explores prior tail the Python engine silently discarded

A-3a, measured early: the performance premise was wrong

This plan claimed the R engine would be roughly 5x faster than Python. Measured on the same 1,398-tick 40-patch default config, same nine components, timing the run plus setup in both:

time per run
Python model.run() + get_parameters() + Model() 0.698 s
R run_LASER_R(), first working version 2.912 s
R run_LASER_R(), after the state-storage fix 1.183 s

Re-measured with the complete ten-component pipeline after A-3: 1.21 s against 1.23 s for the same run without DerivedValues — i.e. the two end-of-run diagnostics cost nothing measurable, because they fire once rather than per tick. The ratio below is unchanged by finishing the port.

So R is 1.69x slower, not 5x faster. The original claim came from a microbenchmark of a representative arithmetic loop, which is exactly the trap §10 warned about and then fell into: it omitted state storage, and state storage turned out to be the cost.

The fix was worth 2.46x on its own. Each channel was a (nticks + 1) x npatches matrix, and a row write state$S[row, ] <- v copies the whole matrix — 15 microseconds against 0.65 for a row read. Line profiling put roughly 55% of the run in those writes, at about 40 of them per tick. Channels are now lists of per-tick vectors, where a write is a pointer store, and the [tick, patch] matrices the results contract needs are assembled once at the end. Allocation fell from 4.9 GB to 987 MB per run. Note that switching the container from a list to an environment, tried first, changed nothing: env$M[i, ] <- v still copies, because fetching M bumps its reference count before the subassignment.

After that the profile is flat — the hottest single line is 6.9% — so there is no second structural win of that size. Closing the remaining 1.69x in pure R would mean many small changes for diminishing returns, or a compiled inner loop, which §10 rules out of scope.

Addendum (v0.73.0, 2026-09-15): the two sentences above are wrong, and the paragraph before them says why. There was a second structural win of that size — 2.25x, larger than the 2.46x fix that prompted this paragraph is worth relative to what remained. The note above is correct that moving the container to an environment “changed nothing … because fetching M bumps its reference count before the subassignment”; what was not carried through is that the replacement structure has the same property. The channels became lists of per-tick vectors but stayed on the state environment, so state$S[[i]] <- v remained a subassignment into an environment-held object and [[<- duplicated the whole nticks + 1 pointer vector on every write. State is now one environment per tick, which is a pointer store with no long vector to copy. The engine is now 0.45 s against the 1.183 s in the table above, so the 1.69x R-vs-Python ratio recorded here no longer holds. The flat profile was not evidence of absence: a per-function profiler charges allocation churn to the line that triggered it and to <GC>. See NEWS.md 0.73.0 and CLAUDE.md lesson 18.

Addendum 2 (v0.73.0, 2026-09-15): the ratio has now been re-measured, and it is the other way round. Interleaved 6 blocks x 3 reps, R v0.73.0 against laser-cholera 0.16.1 in the mo conda env, both reading the SAME inst/extdata/config_default.json, both thread-pinned to 1, Python given an untimed warm-up so numba compilation is not charged to it (harness: claude/perf/1e_xengine.sh + py_arm.py + 1e_r_arm.R, local laptop; raw rows in claude/perf/1e_xengine.txt). Per-block paired ratios, block minima:

arm min mean R faster by (per block)
py_full (get_parameters + Model + run + RInterface) 0.6765 0.7107 —
r071_json (run_simulation(config = <path>)) 0.5810 0.7233 1.15-1.23x
r071_rda (run_simulation(config = <list>)) 0.4000 0.5488 1.65-1.72x

So R is now faster than the Python engine on the like-for-like path, not 1.69x slower, and the “compiled inner loop” conclusion below is moot as a parity argument — it would now be an argument for going faster than the thing we ported from, which is a different decision. Two caveats that matter for reading the table. (i) The spread within an arm across blocks (r071_json min 0.581, mean 0.723) is larger than the gap between the arms, which is exactly why the ratios are quoted per-block and paired and why the unpaired numbers higher up this document should not be compared against these. (ii) The JSON and in-memory arms differ by ~0.18 s of config parsing, against Python’s 0.066 s py_setup. The R arm copies the config to a fresh temp file each rep specifically to defeat the v0.72.0 memoized reader, so 0.18 s is the cold-parse cost; in a calibration the reader is warm and the per-simulation cost is the r071_rda arm. Config parsing, not the tick loop, is now the largest remaining single non-engine cost on the cold path.

This is a decision for the user, not an implementation detail. (Superseded by Addendum 2 above: as of v0.73.0 R is 1.15-1.23x faster on the like-for-like path, so the price below is no longer being paid at all. The rest of this paragraph is kept as the record of the decision as it stood.) At 1.69x, a 40,000-simulation calibration costs about 13 CPU-hours against 8. Against that, the migration still removes reticulate, the ~2 GB-per-worker Python heap (R peaks near 700 MB), the 3.3 s per-worker import, the whole Python environment as a deployment dependency, and the orchestrator/worker version skew that silently invalidated the Coiled runs (issue #113). Whether 1.69x is an acceptable price for that is a judgement about priorities, and the honest position is that the plan oversold it by roughly a factor of 8.

One inventory correction found while verifying C-1. calc_model_ensemble() invoked the Python engine through a closure defined inside its own body, which imported laser.cholera.metapop.model directly rather than going through run_LASER() — a third engine call site, and the one the cutover table (§6) reaches via R/calc_model_ensemble.R:660. That closure is now the package-level .mosaic_ensemble_sim_task() in R/calc_model_ensemble_task.R, so A-4 swaps the engine there in one place instead of editing a closure that PSOCK also clusterExports. The hoist was forced by a subtler problem: precomputed_results= was the seam four test files used to feed synthetic engine output in, and its only production callers were the Dask gather and the Dask medoid dispatch. Deleting the argument silently took 25 assertions with it — on weight/seed alignment, artifact masking and trajectory reduction, all properties of the surviving local path. Mocking the hoisted task restores every one of them and exercises strictly more production code than the argument did, because the task list, the dispatch and the gather now run for real. tests/testthat/helper-ensemble-mock.R holds the seam; parity_tier2.rds still matches bit-for-bit through it, which is the evidence that the hoist changed no arithmetic. Two dead fragments fell out of the same removal, in the shape lesson #14 describes: .spill_traj() (orphaned — its only caller was the removed branch) and the record-carried param_seed tier of the member-seed fallback, which existed only because a Dask worker held a config the master did not.

Next action: none in workstreams A or C — the migration is complete. Every phase is done: the package no longer declares, installs, imports or checks laser-cholera, the engine is pure R, the LASER naming is gone, and acceptance has passed on all four Tier C configs (36/36 bands) and on the calibration comparison (32/32 bands). Two things remain outstanding, and neither blocks the port:

  1. A-3a parallel throughput still needs one clean run on hedgehog or dugong. Everything else the gate asked for is measured and forces no code change — peak RSS is 926 MB/worker, flat from 1 to 19 workers, so memory does not cap worker count. Only the throughput curve is unmeasurable on a hybrid-topology laptop, and it was re-confirmed as unmeasurable here: the A-5 arms ran across a suspend, and the Python harness’s wall-clock timer reported 125 s/sim for work that takes 0.9 s.
  2. weighted_quantiles() had a plotting-position bug — found here, now fixed in v0.71.1. It interpolated against cumsum(w) (the upper edge of each weight block) instead of the midpoint (cumsum(w) - 0.5w)/sum(w), biasing every weighted quantile downward in proportion to how concentrated the weights were. Its own roxygen example (x = 1:5, w = c(.1,.2,.4,.2,.1), symmetric about 3) returned 2.5, and with 99% of the weight on x = 2 it returned 1.49. Equal weights did not reproduce stats::quantile(), and splitting one weight across two copies of the same value changed the answer. Fixed, with regression tests pinning each violated invariance; parity_tier2.rds re-baselined with inputs asserted byte-identical, weighted means confirmed bit-identical at ~4e-16, and every changed cell moving up and none down. The A-5 calibration acceptance was re-run against the fixed function and is unchanged at 32/32 bands — as expected, since both arms were always reduced by the same function. Unrelated to the port; see NEWS 0.71.1.

On the Python-engine comparison the plan asked for. A-5’s text specifies “one full local run_MOSAIC() calibration compared against the last Python-engine run”. No archived Python-engine run is reachable from this machine — there is no MOSAIC root here, get_paths() fails, and neither VM resolves — and C-1 removed the engine="python" path that could regenerate one, so the comparison was inverted instead: the same 500 parameter draws through both engines, scored by the same R likelihood. This is the better-controlled experiment regardless of availability. An archived run would have differed in data vintage, priors version and package version as well as in engine, and those confounds cannot be separated after the fact; here the engine is the only thing that differs. Confirmed with Cliff before proceeding.
